title: SynthFaces: Balanced Large Scale Human Dataset

paper.title: SynthFaces: Balanced Large Scale Human Dataset
paper.abstract: Abstract The pursuit of fair and equitable AI in human-centric tasks is critically hindered by the inherent biases and privacy risks of real-world datasets, which offer imbalanced representations of identity and often contain sensitive personal information. Consequently, state-of-the-art generative models trained on this skewed data exhibit unfair performance, particularly in identity-preserving generation. In this work we propose a pipeline for controllable generation of dataset with diverse faces for generative models training and finetuning. We achieve this by expanding foundational Arc2Face diffusion model with a flow matching generative model in the manifold of identity embeddings. We demonstrate that such approach achieves both goals of generative fidelity and label diversity not present in real human-centric datasets. As a result we collect and further contextualize a highly balanced identity-centric dataset of humans named SynthFaces. By design, our released images and identities are synthetic, reducing direct reliance on real personal images; we empirically check identity separation with a nearest-neighbor non-leakage metric. We purpose it for training and tuning of fair models for various downstream tasks, and showcase its usability in finetuning an existing adapter-based method for personalized generation.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Human image generation is one of the most common applications of modern generative models. The field originated with unconditional generators such as StyleGAN [ 4 ] , which allowed to sample novel faces without any control, and was later expanded to text-to-image diffusion models and adapter-based approaches (e.g., PhotoMaker, SDXL-based personalization), which allow conditioning on a novel face from a single image [ 28 , 36 , 21 , 32 ] and combined with prompt allowed to place human in different context. Unfortunately, most released face-conditional models report averaged quality, which conceals an important aspect of such methods - do they perform equally for different human subgroups ? In this work we show that this is not the case, and try to address this problem with our curated dataset SynthFaces collected with focus on balanced human representation. SynthFaces dataset collection pipeline is designed to address a set of three core problems. 1) Label bias of existing datasets: both existing datasets with human faces, such as FFHQ, SHHQ [ 4 ] , EasyPortrait [ 15 ] and CosmicMan-HQ [ 19 ] and generative samplers exhibit severe category imbalance - both unconditional samplers such as StyleGAN [ 25 ] , as well as by conditional samplers e.g., Arc2Face [ 26 ] , PhotoMaker [ 21 ] produce or reflect skewed distributions over demographic attributes (age, race, gender). 2) Face-similarity quality of conditional samplers: when evaluated per demographic group, conditional personalization models show uneven face preservation quality, which is natural given first problem; 3) Usage of real people identities: existing real datasets, especially large-scale ones, may include identities that did not give consent for deep learning model training or may include identities from under-age groups, using which may be completely unethical and certain datasets have been revoked from public access for that reason [ 13 , 7 ] . Additionally, we aim to fulfill properties that are largely required for modern human-centric datasets - such properties are mentioned in Table 1 , specifically we aim to provide Captions for images, describing both humans and surrounding context, collected images are ID-grouped , meaning that there are multiple images with same person, and lastly we aim to obtain HQ image with high resolution. These properties may be missing for certain types of datasets mentioned in table. For example under Raw Images we denote large-scale raw collections obtained via web-scrapping, are large enough to include all types of faces, however they might still require label-balancing strategy, as well image filtering to obtain high-quality images. HQ Captioned datasets are high quality, but they balance in human representation as we show later, as well as typically do not include multiple images of same person. Face Recognition datasets are typically also without captions, low resolution and also skewed in terms of human representation. In comparison our collected dataset satisfies all of these properties, while also using released images and identities that are synthetic and empirically screened for identity separation. The resulting dataset is balanced across selected demographic labels, ID-grouped, captioned, and contextualized for high-resolution human generation. We systematically study label balance, non-leakage, image quality, and downstream usefulness through generative fine-tuning, face recognition fairness, and demographic VQA in Section 5 .

sections.heading: Synthetic face datasets
sections.text: have been studied primarily for face recognition [ 14 , 1 , 18 ] . Existing pipelines combine GAN samples with per-identity adaptation [ 15 , 29 ] , or exploit the conditional space of face foundation models such as Arc2Face [ 26 ] . HyperFace [ 30 ] explores this hyperspherical space directly, but its generated identities remain demographically imbalanced. Arc2Face and Vec2Face [ 34 ] instead perturb real ArcFace embeddings with PCA, requiring real identity embeddings at inference time and offering no explicit separation from them. ID-Flow learns a controllable prior over the identity manifold, samples without reference embeddings at inference time, and evaluates separation using ID-NonLeak (Table 2 ).

sections.heading: Model fairness
sections.text: seeks to reduce systematic performance differences across demographic subgroups [ 24 , 20 ] . Our approach intervenes at data construction time by controlling the demographic distribution of sampled identities. sections.heading: Identity-preserving generation
sections.text: Identity-preserving generation conditions image synthesis on a reference face. Introduced with adapter-based methods - IP-Adapter-FaceID [ 36 ] , PhotoMaker [ 21 ] , PuLID [ 8 ] , and InstantID [ 32 ] ; InfiniteYou [ 11 ] further improves fidelity and flexibility. Recent in-context models such as Qwen-Image [ 33 ] and Flux-2 [ 17 ] can preserve identity across varied contexts, whereas per-subject methods such as DreamBooth [ 29 ] require fine-tuning for every new identity. We use these models for contextualization after independently controlling the identity distribution.

sections.heading: 3.1 Existing datasets biases
sections.text: To quantify label bias in existing datasets, we annotate them with FairFace classifier [ 12 ] and in Figure 1 show that all of the presented datasets demonstrate heavy bias towards certain labels. Training on such data without empirical balancing strategies can be harmful for generative model fairness and diversity.

sections.heading: 3.2 Evaluating unfairness in human-centric models
sections.text: To expose subgroup differences hidden by aggregate metrics, we construct FairBench , a probe set sampled uniformly over FairFace label combinations. Figure 15 shows substantial demographic variation in identity preservation, consistent with the dataset skew in Figure 1 . Section 5 evaluates whether balanced training data also improves subgroup parity in face recognition and demographic VQA.

sections.heading: 4 Dataset construction
sections.text: In order to build a dataset of synthetic released identities and images, we follow a 3 stage design described in Figure 2 . Each stage is motivated by a specific problem of existing pipelines - at stage 1 we ensure that dataset is private while also free of skewed label distribution, at stage 2 we construct maximum fidelity faces from diverse identity representation, and at stage 3 we achieve high resolution and context coupled with captions.

sections.heading: 4.1 Learning to sample identities

sections.heading: Image statistics filtering
sections.text: we start by analyzing distribution of images characteristics generated by Arc2Face. We evaluate conventional computer vision characteristics of images, such as entropy and saturation . We observe that tail of entropy distribution corresponds to heavily stylized images, low saturation values correspond to black and white images, and high saturation mostly coincides with faces that have unnatural amount of color/light or make up. Therefore we drop around p% of images from tails, removing approximately 3k unsatisfactory images. Qualitative examples are provided in supplementary Figure 11 . Figure 6: Data filtering pipeline from Stage 2 to contextualization - in order to minimize amount of corrupted images with faces we 1) remove images in long tails of statistics 2) detect images with artifacts via vision-language model 3) threshold pairwise similarity, ensuring variability of identities in all categories, resulting in the end with approximately 150,000 final images

sections.heading: VLM filtering
sections.text: After basic image statistics filtering we utilize multiple Qwen-VL models to assess obtained images from two perspectives 1) does the person’s face align with labels that were used to generate them 2) does the person’s face contain any visual artifacts. Based of VLM answers we drop all misaligned images and images that contained faces with visual defects, keeping samples which by majority voting of VLMs are assessed as well-aligned. To make sure that only relevant artifacts are dropped, we prompted VLM to reason about noticed artifacts in the images and dropped images only if the reasoning contained specific key-words. sections.heading: Similarity filtering
sections.text: Additionally, we made sure that resulting identities are not only diverse in terms of labels, but also in terms of embeddings themselves. For that purpose we evaluated distribution of nearest neighbors in the resulting identities and observed a long tail which is not present in typical datasets. After per-label analysis these higher similarity tails occurred for specific label combinations that were particularly rare in training data used for ID-flow training - e.g. rare race groups or age groups. Therefore we filter by similarity threshold for these specific groups, while also keeping a proportion of data across labels close to uniform. After this stage with obtain highly diverse identities, superior to diversity in other baselines - 15 thousand filtered identities and respective labeled images remain. Detailed analysis of this stage results is given in Appendix A.4 . The overall image statistics before and after all filtering strategies applied at this stage are given in Table 4 . Filtering improves image quality metrics (FID e and FID i ) and removes visible artifacts, but it also reduces F1/precision/recall and worsens KL-age because the most problematic tails are not perfectly uniform distributed across demographic labels. sections.heading: Identity contextualization
sections.text: In order to unite curated identities with captions, we utilize state of the art personalization models - InfiniteYou and in-context model Flux 2, first one aims for consistency while second one allows more fidelity and variability. In order to enhance realism of images generated with InfiniteYou we attach additional LoRAs for realism and deblurring, and to speed up generation with Flux 2 we utilize Turbo checkpoint that from experiments turned to be the best amongst existing models for personalized generation of humans, see qualitative comparison in Appendix A.7 . As a result, we obtain a large scale, high quality diverse dataset of synthetic released identities, consisting in total of 150,000 captioned high-resolution images of varying aspect ratios, with approximately 10 images per identity. Resulting samples from this dataset are given in Fig. 7 . Additionally, we evaluate resulting SynthFaces images in terms of image quality by ImageReward(IR) metric [ 35 ] , text alignment by CLIP and ratio of size of face detection box to size of the image side. Compared with the baselines in Table 6 , SynthFaces improves over Cosmic-HQ on ImageReward and CLIP while keeping faces smaller than FluxSynID, whose document-formatted images often lack background context.

sections.heading: 5 Downstream applications
sections.text: We evaluate whether SynthFaces data yields fairness benefits in distinct downstream tasks: finetuning personalized generation pipeline, face recognition (FR) verification and demographic attribute classification. Fine-tuning tests usefulness for id-preserving generation, FR tests whether balanced synthetic identities reduce verification disparity, and VQA tests whether balanced human images help demographic attribute recognition.

sections.text: We measure two core metrics for face preservation on average to observe mean change after adapter tuning, as well as per category analysis - ID - stands for face similarity between source and generated person, CLIP-T - measures similarity between image and prompt description in latent space of CLIP model. sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.text: We use two evaluation benchmarks - one is FairBench introduced before - which is a collection of balanced faces that includes every possible combinations of labels, it’s textual captions focus only on face description. This benchmark corresponds of to maximum reconstruction of person facial features. Second benchmark named Context is a less diverse in terms of labels, but includes richer prompts specializing in placing people in contexts, demonstrating trade-off between face similarity being lower for smaller faces and more contextualized humans. sections.heading: Training details
sections.text: Finetuning conditional diffusion model comes with a challenge of data distribution drift . It’s a problem that arises because of discrepancy between data that was used for training original checkpoint and data that is being used for finetuning. Main characteristic that seemingly may hurt performance of these methods in terms of face preservation is learned face size . Face size in collected data serves as hidden factor that can be learned by diffusion model and directly affect similarity metric. Therefore to mitigate effect of this hidden factor we apply approach from [ 5 ] termed shortcut finetuning - specifically we attach frozen ControlNet [ 37 ] to condition on human pose and face position in source image, making finetuned IP-adapter layers learn only essential features related to face preservation. Details about this approach and hyperparameters for training are given in Appendix A.8 . We provide finetuning results for StableDiffusion coupled with IPAdapter-FaceID. We observe a significant mean improvement in fair face reconstruction benchmark, while keeping comparable performance of contextualized generation. However, it is also important to inspect the change in quality per label. In Fig. 8 we showcase improvement across different label values per age and race groups - improvement is not isolated and ultimately makes performance more uniform. More detailed finetuning results with another personalized generation method are provided in Appendix A.8 .

sections.heading: Setup
sections.text: We train FR model on a version of our synthetic dataset purposed for this task - we sample 500k images from ID-Flow + Arc2Face with uniform labels, 50 images per identity, and additionally filter identities by similarity threshold in every subgroup. We compare with two other available FR model baselines: SynthFaces-500K (IResNet-100, ArcFace, ∼ \sim 500K images of 10K identities from our pipeline), Vec2Face [ 34 ] (IResNet-50 SE, ArcFace, ∼ \sim 300K images, HSFace300K real-web source), and HyperFace [ 30 ] . We evaluate on two regimes: (a) five standard FR benchmarks (LFW, CFP-FP, AgeDB-30, CALFW, CPLFW) annotated post-hoc with FairFace [ 12 ] demographic labels, and (b) BFW (Balanced Faces in the Wild) [ 27 ] , a balanced dataset with over ∼ \sim 900K images balanced across 4 races × \times 2 genders with human-assigned labels.

sections.heading: Fairness metrics
sections.text: We aim to evaluate fairness of trained FR models. After analyzing standard FR benchmarks we find them to be heavily skewed (AgeDB-30: 88% White; LFW: 66% White, 75% male - see Table 14 in the Appendix), making accuracy-disparity metrics conflate representation with bias. A face verification system accepts or rejects a pair against a threshold τ \tau ; the two governing error rates are the False Match Rate (FMR) and False Non-Match Rate (FNMR) [ 6 ] . We evaluate at a calibrated operating point: fix the global FMR to target α ∈ { 1 % , 0.1 % } \alpha\in\{1\%,0.1\%\} via τ α = Quantile α ​ ( { D i : y i = 0 } ) \tau_{\alpha}=\text{Quantile}_{\alpha}(\{D_{i}:y_{i}{=}0\}) , then measure per-group FNMR. This reflects realistic deployment where an operator fixes a tolerable false-alarm rate. To normalize for absolute model quality and isolate relative group (dis)advantage, we adopt the Skewed Error Ratio (SER), inspired by [ 31 ] : SER g ​ ( α ) = FNMR g ​ ( α ) FNMR global ​ ( α ) . \text{SER}_{g}(\alpha)=\frac{\text{FNMR}_{g}(\alpha)}{\text{FNMR}_{\text{global}}(\alpha)}. SER = 1.0 \text{SER}=1.0 is perfect parity; SER > 1 \text{SER}>1 indicates disproportionate miss burden. We report SER max = max g ⁡ SER g \text{SER}_{\max}=\max_{g}\text{SER}_{g} (lower = fairer). sections.heading: Setup
sections.text: We fine-tune LLaVA-1.5-7B [ 23 ] with LoRA adapters on demographic VQA data from three sources: (a) SynthFaces-HQ - samples from our datasets paired with multiple-choice questions on gender, race, and age derived from pipeline annotations; (b) SynthFaces - mirrors HQ version, but uses non-HQ images with just human faces (c) Vec2Face - a VQA set from arc2face-rendered images annotated with FairFace labels. All runs follow an identical LoRA fine-tuning protocol; checkpoints are selected by fairness/accuracy trade-off on a held-out split.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced SynthFaces, a large-scale, identity-grouped and captioned synthetic human dataset designed for demographic balance while reducing reliance on released images of real individuals. Its ID-Flow sampler provides explicit demographic control while maintaining identity diversity and empirical separation from the real identities used for training. Across personalized generation, face recognition, and demographic VQA, models trained with SynthFaces improve subgroup parity while retaining useful task performance. These results show that controlling identity composition during dataset construction is an effective lever for fairer human-centric models. Future work should reduce dependence on potentially biased face encoders and foundation generators and investigate hybrid real–synthetic balancing strategies.

sections.heading: 7 Limitations
sections.text: While SynthFaces addresses key gaps in existing datasets, several limitations should be acknowledged.

sections.heading: Bias inheritance from foundation models.
sections.text: Arc2Face and Flux despite being state of the art generators for corresponding parts of pipeline carry aesthetic and demographic biases from their respective training corpora. Our pipeline guarantees label-level balance across age, race, and gender, but within-group visual diversity and image style remain bounded by what these upstream models can faithfully generate. Demographic combinations that are underrepresented in Arc2Face’s training data may yield lower-fidelity or less varied outputs.

sections.heading: Synthetic-to-real distribution gap.
sections.text: Images produced by diffusion models may contain subtle distributional artifacts absent from real photographs. While our VLM-based filtering step removes overt defects, residual domain differences could limit transferability when SynthFaces-trained models are evaluated on real-world data.

sections.heading: Dependency on upstream model capabilities.
sections.text: The expressive range of generated identities is ultimately constrained by Arc2Face’s capacity for identity preservation and Flux’s generation quality. Improvements to either foundation model would directly benefit downstream dataset quality, but also introduce a moving dependency.

sections.heading: 8 Ethics statement
sections.text: The creation of SynthFaces is a direct response to the ethical crisis surrounding web-scraped human-centric datasets, many of which have been rightfully retracted due to non-consensual use of personal images, including those of minors. To reduce these privacy and consent risks, SynthFaces releases synthetic identities generated by our pipeline rather than scraped personal images. Because ID-Flow is trained from ArcFace embeddings extracted from real datasets, we do not claim a formal privacy guarantee; instead, we empirically evaluate nearest-neighbor separation with the ID-NonLeak metric and design the dataset to avoid direct re-use of real personal images. Furthermore, we address the issue of demographic bias that plagues both real and synthetic datasets. Our pipeline is explicitly designed to generate a balanced representation across age, gender, and ethnicity, creating a resource purposed for training fairer models and mitigating the harmful disparities common in existing technologies. While we acknowledge that no synthetic data is perfect and subtle biases may persist, we believe this work demonstrates a responsible path forward, decoupling progress in human-centric computer vision from the exploitation of personal data.

sections.heading: Data collection
sections.text: Our training stage is conducted fully in latent space of ArcFace embedding. To obtain them, we first processed images from Cosmic-HQ, FFHQ, EasyPortait and also enriched with images of people from the internet. We included only embeddings that were detectable with fixed bounding box size set to 640, since embeddings tend to significantly differ depending on detection size. We implement a deduplication stage, where all collected embeddings are filtered out by a threshold value of 0.4 pairwise cosine similarity, ensuring diverse faces are used for training and avoiding identity collapse, where model learns only fixed amount of identities. Then we also annotate all collected images with FairFace, providing age/race/gender labels, and remove embeddings that correspond to images that failed labeling stage. As a result, we train on around 50k identity embeddings with labels. For evaluation we use hold-out set of Cosmic-HQ images and CelebA, which weren’t used during training, and apply same pipeline to obtain embeddings and labels, without deduplication stage.

sections.heading: A.6 Label matching captions with HQ images
sections.text: In Algorithms 1 and 2 we describe two-stage strategy to match captions of real images with labels of identities. Firstly, we define a finite set of groups that we classify captions into - these groups are mainly defined by age and gender, e.g. adult_male and child_female , and then we collect a final collection of captions for identities by sampling from appropriate group depending on label values of identity. Race labels are intentionally not used for caption matching, so that contextual prompts do not encode race-specific descriptors. This approach has two advantages 1) its algorithmic cost is O ⁡ ( n + m ) O(n+m) , where n n is number of processed captions and m m number of processed labels 2) it allows to avoid heavy cases where captions are not suitable for identity, avoiding synthesizing controversial or unnatural content. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.40119v1 [cs.CV] 29 Oct 2026 SynthFaces SynthFaces: Balanced Large Scale Human Dataset Sergey Karpukhin Denis Bobkov Kirill Morozov Aibek Alanov Abstract The pursuit of fair and equitable AI in human-centric tasks is critically hindered by the inherent biases and privacy risks of real-world datasets, which offer imbalanced representations of identity and often contain sensitive personal information. Consequently, state-of-the-art generative models trained on this skewed data exhibit unfair performance, particularly in identity-preserving generation. In this work we propose a pipeline for controllable generation of dataset with diverse faces for generative models training and finetuning. We achieve this by expanding foundational Arc2Face diffusion model with a flow matching generative model in the manifold of identity embeddings. We demonstrate that such approach achieves both goals of generative fidelity and label diversity not present in real human-centric datasets. As a result we collect and further contextualize a highly balanced identity-centric dataset of humans named SynthFaces. By design, our released images and identities are synthetic, reducing direct reliance on real personal images; we empirically check identity separation with a nearest-neighbor non-leakage metric. We purpose it for training and tuning of fair models for various downstream tasks, and showcase its usability in finetuning an existing adapter-based method for personalized generation. keywords empty dictionary keywords return keywords empty list keywords return † † email: seriy.karp2@gmail.com † † email: dbobkov@hse.ru † † email: s02230196@gse.cs.msu.ru † † email: aalanov@hse.ru † † affiliation: FusionBrain Lab, AXXX Moscow, Russia † † affiliation: HSE University Moscow, Russia † † affiliation: MSU Moscow, Russia 1 Introduction Human image generation is one of the most common applications of modern generative models. The field originated with unconditional generators such as StyleGAN [ 4 ] , which allowed to sample novel faces without any control, and was later expanded to text-to-image diffusion models and adapter-based approaches (e.g., PhotoMaker, SDXL-based personalization), which allow conditioning on a novel face from a single image [ 28 , 36 , 21 , 32 ] and combined with prompt allowed to place human in different context. Unfortunately, most released face-conditional models report averaged quality, which conceals an important aspect of such methods - do they perform equally for different human subgroups ? In this work we show that this is not the case, and try to address this problem with our curated dataset SynthFaces collected with focus on balanced human representation. SynthFaces dataset collection pipeline is designed to address a set of three core problems. 1) Label bias of existing datasets: both existing datasets with human faces, such as FFHQ, SHHQ [ 4 ] , EasyPortrait [ 15 ] and CosmicMan-HQ [ 19 ] and generative samplers exhibit severe category imbalance - both unconditional samplers such as StyleGAN [ 25 ] , as well as by conditional samplers e.g., Arc2Face [ 26 ] , PhotoMaker [ 21 ] produce or reflect skewed distributions over demographic attributes (age, race, gender). 2) Face-similarity quality of conditional samplers: when evaluated per demographic group, conditional personalization models show uneven face preservation quality, which is natural given first problem; 3) Usage of real people identities: existing real datasets, especially large-scale ones, may include identities that did not give consent for deep learning model training or may include identities from under-age groups, using which may be completely unethical and certain datasets have been revoked from public access for that reason [ 13 , 7 ] . Additionally, we aim to fulfill properties that are largely required for modern human-centric datasets - such properties are mentioned in Table 1 , specifically we aim to provide Captions for images, describing both humans and surrounding context, collected images are ID-grouped , meaning that there are multiple images with same person, and lastly we aim to obtain HQ image with high resolution. These properties may be missing for certain types of datasets mentioned in table. For example under Raw Images we denote large-scale raw collections obtained via web-scrapping, are large enough to include all types of faces, however they might still require label-balancing strategy, as well image filtering to obtain high-quality images. HQ Captioned datasets are high quality, but they balance in human representation as we show later, as well as typically do not include multiple images of same person. Face Recognition datasets are typically also without captions, low resolution and also skewed in terms of human representation. In comparison our collected dataset satisfies all of these properties, while also using released images and identities that are synthetic and empirically screened for identity separation. Table 1: High level comparison of dataset types, in columns Caption denotes that images are paired with prompts, Balanced labels that dataset is balanced over selected demographic labels, ID-grouped that multiple images per person are provided and HQ suggests that images are high resolution and visually high quality Type Dataset Captions Balanced labels ID-grouped Private HQ Raw Images VGG-Face, WebFace no partially yes no partially HQ Captioned Cosmic, DeepFashion yes no no no yes Face Recognition DCFace, HyperFace no no yes partially no SynthFaces (ours) yes yes yes yes yes SynthFaces addresses these problems by introducing controllable label diversity into identity representation sampling and by releasing synthetic identities whose separation from real training identities is checked through ID-NonLeak. The resulting dataset is balanced across selected demographic labels, ID-grouped, captioned, and contextualized for high-resolution human generation. We systematically study label balance, non-leakage, image quality, and downstream usefulness through generative fine-tuning, face recognition fairness, and demographic VQA in Section 5 . 2 Related Works Synthetic face datasets have been studied primarily for face recognition [ 14 , 1 , 18 ] . Existing pipelines combine GAN samples with per-identity adaptation [ 15 , 29 ] , or exploit the conditional space of face foundation models such as Arc2Face [ 26 ] . HyperFace [ 30 ] explores this hyperspherical space directly, but its generated identities remain demographically imbalanced. Arc2Face and Vec2Face [ 34 ] instead perturb real ArcFace embeddings with PCA, requiring real identity embeddings at inference time and offering no explicit separation from them. ID-Flow learns a controllable prior over the identity manifold, samples without reference embeddings at inference time, and evaluates separation using ID-NonLeak (Table 2 ). Model fairness seeks to reduce systematic performance differences across demographic subgroups [ 24 , 20 ] . Our approach intervenes at data construction time by controlling the demographic distribution of sampled identities. Figure 1: Distribution of labels across different categories in some of conventional datasets with humans. Dashed lines denotes mean value across labels, color highlights values above mean Identity-preserving generation Identity-preserving generation conditions image synthesis on a reference face. Introduced with adapter-based methods - IP-Adapter-FaceID [ 36 ] , PhotoMaker [ 21 ] , PuLID [ 8 ] , and InstantID [ 32 ] ; InfiniteYou [ 11 ] further improves fidelity and flexibility. Recent in-context models such as Qwen-Image [ 33 ] and Flux-2 [ 17 ] can preserve identity across varied contexts, whereas per-subject methods such as DreamBooth [ 29 ] require fine-tuning for every new identity. We use these models for contextualization after independently controlling the identity distribution. 3 Motivation 3.1 Existing datasets biases To quantify label bias in existing datasets, we annotate them with FairFace classifier [ 12 ] and in Figure 1 show that all of the presented datasets demonstrate heavy bias towards certain labels. Training on such data without empirical balancing strategies can be harmful for generative model fairness and diversity. 3.2 Evaluating unfairness in human-centric models To expose subgroup differences hidden by aggregate metrics, we construct FairBench , a probe set sampled uniformly over FairFace label combinations. Figure 15 shows substantial demographic variation in identity preservation, consistent with the dataset skew in Figure 1 . Section 5 evaluates whether balanced training data also improves subgroup parity in face recognition and demographic VQA. 4 Dataset construction In order to build a dataset of synthetic released identities and images, we follow a 3 stage design described in Figure 2 . Each stage is motivated by a specific problem of existing pipelines - at stage 1 we ensure that dataset is private while also free of skewed label distribution, at stage 2 we construct maximum fidelity faces from diverse identity representation, and at stage 3 we achieve high resolution and context coupled with captions. 4.1 Learning to sample identities Identity embeddings lie on a unit hypersphere, so treating them as unconstrained Euclidean vectors ignores their geometry. We instead learn a geodesic flow-matching model directly on this manifold. Figure 2: Dataset multi-stage collection pipeline. We aim to train a generative model in latent space of identity embeddings. Natural observation is that these embeddings are all unit length and therefore exists on a n n -dimensional sphere. Some prior works tried to explore this idea, for example in [ 30 ] authors pose problem of sampling diverse embeddings as optimization problem on sphere, and in [ 3 ] authors construct von Mises–Fisher based diffusion model that respects manifold geometry. In this work we make a novel adaptation of non-Euclidean flow matching to construct a generative model on identity latents. These embeddings as noted by Stage 2 plan, are turned into face images, and various filtering strategies are applied in order to enhance output of this stage and get rid of potential artifacts present in images. Image statistics filtering we start by analyzing distribution of images characteristics generated by Arc2Face. We evaluate conventional computer vision characteristics of images, such as entropy and saturation . We observe that tail of entropy distribution corresponds to heavily stylized images, low saturation values correspond to black and white images, and high saturation mostly coincides with faces that have unnatural amount of color/light or make up. Therefore we drop around p% of images from tails, removing approximately 3k unsatisfactory images. Qualitative examples are provided in supplementary Figure 11 . We filtered prompts to exclude any details related to attributes that were controlled during identity sampling, including details with description of facial features. After that we roughly annotated these captions into subgroups based of their context, main factor being suitable age, e.g. prompts for child, prompts for adults, etc. After that we randomly sampled captions for each image given its label, matching label with classes with captions that are suitable for these face label values by looking for specific keywords that were used as person descriptors. Identity contextualization In order to unite curated identities with captions, we utilize state of the art personalization models - InfiniteYou and in-context model Flux 2, first one aims for consistency while second one allows more fidelity and variability. In order to enhance realism of images generated with InfiniteYou we attach additional LoRAs for realism and deblurring, and to speed up generation with Flux 2 we utilize Turbo checkpoint that from experiments turned to be the best amongst existing models for personalized generation of humans, see qualitative comparison in Appendix A.7 . As a result, we obtain a large scale, high quality diverse dataset of synthetic released identities, consisting in total of 150,000 captioned high-resolution images of varying aspect ratios, with approximately 10 images per identity. Resulting samples from this dataset are given in Fig. 7 . Additionally, we evaluate resulting SynthFaces images in terms of image quality by ImageReward(IR) metric [ 35 ] , text alignment by CLIP and ratio of size of face detection box to size of the image side. Compared with the baselines in Table 6 , SynthFaces improves over Cosmic-HQ on ImageReward and CLIP while keeping faces smaller than FluxSynID, whose document-formatted images often lack background context. 5 Downstream applications We evaluate whether SynthFaces data yields fairness benefits in distinct downstream tasks: finetuning personalized generation pipeline, face recognition (FR) verification and demographic attribute classification. Fine-tuning tests usefulness for id-preserving generation, FR tests whether balanced synthetic identities reduce verification disparity, and VQA tests whether balanced human images help demographic attribute recognition. 5.1 ID-preserving generation Metrics We measure two core metrics for face preservation on average to observe mean change after adapter tuning, as well as per category analysis - ID - stands for face similarity between source and generated person, CLIP-T - measures similarity between image and prompt description in latent space of CLIP model. Figure 8: Face similarity measured across different categories of IpAdapter-FaceID before and after tuning on data generated by ID-flow. Evaluation We use two evaluation benchmarks - one is FairBench introduced before - which is a collection of balanced faces that includes every possible combinations of labels, it’s textual captions focus only on face description. This benchmark corresponds of to maximum reconstruction of person facial features. Second benchmark named Context is a less diverse in terms of labels, but includes richer prompts specializing in placing people in contexts, demonstrating trade-off between face similarity being lower for smaller faces and more contextualized humans. Table 7: Effect of tuning pipelines with our dataset, reporting average metric values FairBench Context Method ID CLIP-T ID CLIP-T SD-1.5 + FaceID 68.63 32.91 28.81 53.56 SD-1.5 + FaceID (+ tuned) 71.31 33.27 28.49 51.56 Training details Finetuning conditional diffusion model comes with a challenge of data distribution drift . It’s a problem that arises because of discrepancy between data that was used for training original checkpoint and data that is being used for finetuning. Main characteristic that seemingly may hurt performance of these methods in terms of face preservation is learned face size . Face size in collected data serves as hidden factor that can be learned by diffusion model and directly affect similarity metric. Therefore to mitigate effect of this hidden factor we apply approach from [ 5 ] termed shortcut finetuning - specifically we attach frozen ControlNet [ 37 ] to condition on human pose and face position in source image, making finetuned IP-adapter layers learn only essential features related to face preservation. Details about this approach and hyperparameters for training are given in Appendix A.8 . We provide finetuning results for StableDiffusion coupled with IPAdapter-FaceID. We observe a significant mean improvement in fair face reconstruction benchmark, while keeping comparable performance of contextualized generation. However, it is also important to inspect the change in quality per label. Its ID-Flow sampler provides explicit demographic control while maintaining identity diversity and empirical separation from the real identities used for training. Across personalized generation, face recognition, and demographic VQA, models trained with SynthFaces improve subgroup parity while retaining useful task performance. These results show that controlling identity composition during dataset construction is an effective lever for fairer human-centric models. Future work should reduce dependence on potentially biased face encoders and foundation generators and investigate hybrid real–synthetic balancing strategies. 7 Limitations While SynthFaces addresses key gaps in existing datasets, several limitations should be acknowledged. Bias inheritance from foundation models. Arc2Face and Flux despite being state of the art generators for corresponding parts of pipeline carry aesthetic and demographic biases from their respective training corpora. Our pipeline guarantees label-level balance across age, race, and gender, but within-group visual diversity and image style remain bounded by what these upstream models can faithfully generate. Demographic combinations that are underrepresented in Arc2Face’s training data may yield lower-fidelity or less varied outputs. Synthetic-to-real distribution gap. Images produced by diffusion models may contain subtle distributional artifacts absent from real photographs. While our VLM-based filtering step removes overt defects, residual domain differences could limit transferability when SynthFaces-trained models are evaluated on real-world data. Dependency on upstream model capabilities. The expressive range of generated identities is ultimately constrained by Arc2Face’s capacity for identity preservation and Flux’s generation quality. Improvements to either foundation model would directly benefit downstream dataset quality, but also introduce a moving dependency. 8 Ethics statement The creation of SynthFaces is a direct response to the ethical crisis surrounding web-scraped human-centric datasets, many of which have been rightfully retracted due to non-consensual use of personal images, including those of minors. To reduce these privacy and consent risks, SynthFaces releases synthetic identities generated by our pipeline rather than scraped personal images. Because ID-Flow is trained from ArcFace embeddings extracted from real datasets, we do not claim a formal privacy guarantee; instead, we empirically evaluate nearest-neighbor separation with the ID-NonLeak metric and design the dataset to avoid direct re-use of real personal images. Furthermore, we address the issue of demographic bias that plagues both real and synthetic datasets. Our pipeline is explicitly designed to generate a balanced representation across age, gender, and ethnicity, creating a resource purposed for training fairer models and mitigating the harmful disparities common in existing technologies. While we acknowledge that no synthetic data is perfect and subtle biases may persist, we believe this work demonstrates a responsible path forward, decoupling progress in human-centric computer vision from the exploitation of personal data. 9 Acknowledgment We gratefully acknowledge HSE University for providing access to its computational cluster, which was used to conduct the experiments presented in this work.
